name: Cutting sugar for gums
lead: Cutting sugar for gums is the practice of reducing dietary sugar with the aim of lowering dental plaque and improving gum health. Proponents reason that plaque bacteria feed on sugars.

Gingivitis is described as caused mainly by bacterial plaque, with brushing and flossing as the main prevention measures.[1] That article does not address diet. Reference text on remineralisation notes that plaque removal and reduced frequency of sugar intake support enamel repair and that some studies show a link between sugar and tooth decay.[2]
infobox: None found specific to gum outcomes in this entry

paras: The practice involves eating less added sugar, with the stated goal of giving plaque bacteria less to ferment. Plaque-induced gingivitis arises from bacterial biofilm on teeth, and other listed risk factors include poor oral hygiene, smoking, diabetes and pregnancy.[1]
Standard prevention advice focuses on daily brushing and flossing.[1] For tooth decay, plaque removal and reduced sugar frequency are described as supporting remineralisation.[2]

card.summary: Eating less sugar to starve plaque bacteria; linked to cavities in research, but gum-specific trials are not found here.
card.note: Does not replace brushing, flossing or dental care.

quick.overview:
This is the idea of reducing sugar intake to reduce plaque and gum problems. It is a general dietary practice rather than a product.

Sources found link sugar to tooth decay in some studies; no trials specific to gums were found.
quick.mechanism: Plaque bacteria release toxins that inflame gums, and the practice aims to reduce the sugar those bacteria use.
quick.risks: No specific risks are documented. Dental guidance centres on brushing and flossing.
